statement: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.
heath_proof: For in the circle ABCD let the two straight lines AC, BD cut one another at the point E; I say that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. If now AC, BD are through the centre, so that E is the centre of the circle ABCD, it is manifest that, AE, EC, DE, EB being equal, the rectangle contained by AE, EC is also equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Next let AC, DB not be through the centre; let the centre of ABCD be taken, and let it be F; from F let FG, FH be drawn perpendicular to the straight lines AC, DB, and let FB, FC, FE be joined. Then, since a straight line GF through the centre cuts a straight line AC not through the centre at right angles, it also bisects it; [III. 3]therefore AG is equal to GC. Since, then, the straight line AC has been cut into equal parts at G and into unequal parts at E, the rectangle contained by AE, EC together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GC; [II. 5] Let the square on GF be added; therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the squares on GE, GF is equal to the squares on CG, GF. But the square on FE is equal to the squares on EG, GF, and the square on FC is equal to the squares on CG, GF; [I. 47] therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FC.  And FC is equal to FB; therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FB. For the same reason, also, the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FB. But the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE was also proved equal to the square on FB; therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on FE is equal to the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on FE. Let the square on FE be subtracted from each; therefore the rectangle contained by AE, EC which remains is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB.

**Statement:** If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a circle, and in it let the two straight lines AC and BD cut one another at the point E. We must show that the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Take the centre F of the circle [3.1].

**Step 2.** First, suppose that E is the centre F. Then AE, EC, DE, EB are all drawn from the centre to the circumference, so they are equal to one another [D1.15]. Hence the rectangle AE, EC is the square on AE, the rectangle DE, EB is the square on DE, and since AE = DE these squares are equal. So the two rectangles are equal, and the proposition holds in this case.

**Step 3.** Next, suppose that E is not the centre F. We first establish the following for either of the two given straight lines: if XY is one of them (X, Y being its extremities on the circumference) and E the point on it at which they cut, then the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. Join FX [P1].

**Step 4.** Case (a): XY passes through the centre F. Then FX = FY, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference [D1.15], so XY is bisected at F; and since E is not F, XY is cut into unequal segments at E. Therefore, XY being cut into equal segments at F and into unequal segments at E, the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on FE is equal to the square on the half, that is, on FX [2.5]. This is the required equation.

**Step 5.** Case (b): XY does not pass through F. From F draw FG perpendicular to XY [1.12], so that the angles at G are right [D1.10]. Since FG is a straight line through the centre which cuts the straight line XY, not through the centre, at right angles, it also bisects it [3.3]; therefore XG = GY.

**Step 6.** Suppose E does not coincide with G. Then XY is cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at E; therefore the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GX [2.5]. Add the square on GF to each: the rectangle XE, EY together with the squares on EG, GF is equal to the squares on GX, GF [CN2].

**Step 7.** In the triangle EGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on EG, GF are equal to the square on FE; and in the triangle XGF the angle at G is right, so the squares on GX, GF are equal to the square on FX [1.47]. Hence, from Step 6, the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on FE is equal to the square on FX [CN1].

**Step 8.** If instead E coincides with G, then XE = EY, so the rectangle XE, EY is the square on XE; and FE is the perpendicular FG, so in the right-angled triangle XEF the square on XE together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX [1.47]. Thus again the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX.

**Step 9.** Therefore in every case (Steps 4 to 8) the rectangle XE, EY together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FX. Applying this to the straight line AC: the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FA. Applying it to the straight line BD: the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on EF is equal to the square on FB.

**Step 10.** But FA = FB, both being drawn from the centre to the circumference [D1.15], so the square on FA is equal to the square on FB. Therefore the rectangle AE, EC together with the square on EF is equal to the rectangle DE, EB together with the square on EF [CN1].

**Step 11.** Subtract the square on EF from each: the rectangle AE, EC is equal to the rectangle DE, EB [CN3].

**Step 12.** Therefore, combining Step 2 with Step 11, in every case the rectangle contained by AE, EC is equal to the rectangle contained by DE, EB. Q.E.D.
